items.title: Which Check proves GetByIdAsync returns deleted rows
items.body:
To prove that `GetByIdAsync` returns soft-deleted rows, you cite its default parameter, `includeDeleted = true`, and the filter helper it would otherwise use, then find a caller that relies on the default (order history) and one that overrides it.

- Finding the builder line or type-table entry for `Sku` and `Price` belongs to predicting column types.
- Filling in the atomicity table from memory belongs to classifying repository writes.

items.title: Why two nodes can both take the lock
items.body:
`PerformActionWithLockAsync` first calls `GetStringAsync(resource)` and returns false if a value exists. Only afterwards does it call `SetStringAsync`. Those are two separate round trips to the cache. Two nodes that both read before either writes both see an empty key, both set it and both run the task. An atomic set-if-absent with a per-holder token would close the gap.

- `SetStringAsync` overwrites; it has no only-if-absent mode here.
- The cache server runs each call separately, not the whole method.
- Both nodes read before either writes, so neither sees a lock.

items.title: Which Check settles lockout on a fresh install
items.body:
Whether lockout is on after installation is settled by two lines: the installer's `FailedPasswordAllowedAttempts = 0` and the `> 0` guard in the wrong-password branch of `ValidateCustomerAsync`. Together they show the lock branch cannot run until an admin changes the setting.

- Listing gates 4 to 9 from memory proves the gate order, not the default.
- Following `[CheckPermission]` to its cache key traces a permission check.

items.title: Why lockout never triggers on a fresh install
items.body:
The installer writes `FailedPasswordAllowedAttempts = 0`. In the wrong-password branch the code first runs `customer.FailedLoginAttempts++`, then locks out only if the setting is `> 0` and the counter has reached it. With 0 the lock condition is false, so the customer is never locked out, while the counter keeps rising on every failure.

- No five-attempt default exists; the installer value is 0.
- 0 does not mean lock on the first failure; it disables the branch.
- Counting is not switched off; the increment comes before the check.

items.title: Which Check proves you know the login gate order
items.body:
Reproducing the gate order means listing gates 4 to 9 from `ValidateCustomerAsync` without the table, then comparing: lookup, deleted, inactive, not registered, lockout, password, MFA and success bookkeeping in the order the method runs them.

- Following `[CheckPermission]` to its cache key belongs to tracing a permission check.
- Citing the installer value and the `> 0` guard belongs to deciding whether lockout is on.

items.title: Start here: three chapters on a 15-year-old shop
items.body:
nopCommerce is a large open-source ASP.NET Core MVC e-commerce platform. Its code is in `nopCommerce/src`: three libraries (`Nop.Core`, `Nop.Data`, `Nop.Services`) under two web projects (`Nop.Web` and `Nop.Web.Framework`). The repository is far too big to read end to end, and you do not need to build it: this quest is about reading.

The curriculum lives in `nopCommerce/fabledocs/`. Use three chapters of `03-architecture-and-patterns/`:

1. `02-data-model-and-persistence.md`: repository semantics, soft delete, transactions, schema defaults.
2. `03-validation-auth-and-permissions.md`: the login gates and permission layers.
3. `04-side-effects-async-and-reliability.md`: events, scheduled tasks and locks.

Each chapter has the same parts: a map, a feature trace, an **Exercise ladder** of Goal and Check pairs, **Senior findings**, a debugging scenario and a verification note. Every claim carries a `file#Lline` anchor into `src/`; open the anchors rather than trusting the summary. Some quiz items are the exercise ladder itself: for each Goal, know which Check proves it.

items.title: Concept: persistence without a unit of work
items.body:
If you know EF Core, nopCommerce's data layer will surprise you. It uses Linq2Db with a generic `EntityRepository<T>`, and there is no change tracker and no unit of work: each repository call opens its own connection and runs its own statement. Whether two writes succeed or fail together depends entirely on whether something wrapped them in a `TransactionScope`.

Two more ideas recur. **Soft delete** marks a row as deleted instead of removing it, so history that points at the row still resolves; the price is that every read must decide whether it wants deleted rows. **Schema by convention** means the table definition comes from C# types plus a few explicit overrides.

What to look for in `Nop.Data/EntityRepository.cs`:

- the default value of every optional parameter on `GetByIdAsync`;
- which of the list overloads call `CreateTransactionScope`, and how `BaseDataProvider` implements the others;
- how the two `DeleteAsync` overloads (entity and predicate) treat `ISoftDeletedEntity`, and which one calls the event publisher.

Then read the `TypeMapping` table and the `ForeignKey` helper in `FluentMigratorExtensions.cs`.

excerpts.quote: There is **no unit of work**: two repository calls in a service are two independent statements unless an ambient `TransactionScope` wraps them.

items.title: Why the slow runner deletes the other node's lock
items.body:
For an hourly task the lock lifetime is `Math.Min(Seconds, 300) - 1` = 299 seconds, so after five minutes the key expires while A is still working. B then sets the key and starts. When A finishes, its `finally` calls `RemoveAsync(resource)` with no check of who set the key. The stored value is just the resource name, so there is no owner to compare. A deletes B's lock.

- The `finally` always removes the key.
- No owner token exists, so nothing can detect a mismatch.
- Nothing extends a lock; expiry is fixed when the key is set.

items.title: Which Check proves the lock-lifetime goal
items.body:
The goal is to compute how long a task's lock lives. The matching Check works the formula on two periods: `Seconds = 60` gives a 59-second lock and `Seconds = 3600` gives 299 seconds, from `Math.Min(Seconds, 300) - 1` in `ScheduleTaskRunner`.

- The grep for `IConsumer<OrderPlacedEvent>` belongs to the goal of listing synchronous checkout work.
- Pointing at the `try/catch` in `EventPublisher` proves that a publish never throws to its caller.

items.title: Why the right password still gets LockedOut
items.body:
`ValidateCustomerAsync` checks the lockout window, `CannotLoginUntilDateUtc > DateTime.UtcNow`, before it compares passwords. A customer inside the window gets `LockedOut` whatever they type, and the success branch that clears the timestamp is never reached. The guide's debugging scenario uses the same fact: a stale lockout timestamp survives until a successful login, which the locked customer cannot reach.

- The correct password is never checked, so it cannot clear anything.
- WrongPassword is returned only after a failed comparison.
- MFA is checked after the password, which is never reached here.

items.title: Which Check proves you classified repository writes
items.body:
Classifying every repository write by atomicity is done by filling in the semantics table yourself from `EntityRepository` lines 340 to 506, then comparing with the guide: which overloads use `CreateTransactionScope`, which are single statements, and which loop without a transaction.

- Citing `includeDeleted = true` proves the soft-delete default of `GetByIdAsync`.
- Finding the builder line for `Sku` and `Price` predicts column types.

items.title: Why a failing consumer never reaches checkout
items.body:
`PublishAsync` resolves every consumer and awaits them one by one, each inside its own `try`. A `catch` logs `exception.Message` through `ILogger` and the `foreach` moves on to the next consumer. Nothing is rethrown, so the caller (here `PlaceOrderAsync`) sees a normal completion. The guide sums it up: a publish never fails from the caller's point of view.

- Nothing is rethrown, before or after the loop.
- There is no aggregation of errors; each one is logged on its own.
- Repository calls run their own statements, so there is no shared transaction to roll back.

excerpts.quote: Consequence: a publish *never fails* from the caller's point of view.

items.title: Which Check predicts column types
items.body:
Predicting a column's SQL type without running a migration means finding the rule that decides it. For `Product.Sku` that is the builder line, `AsString(400).Nullable()`. For `Product.Price` no builder line exists, so the type table's `decimal` entry, `AsDecimal(18, 4)`, applies.

- Filling in the atomicity table belongs to classifying repository writes.
- Citing `includeDeleted = true` belongs to the soft-delete goal.

items.title: Why the predicate delete is a silent hard delete
items.body:
The predicate overload of `DeleteAsync` calls `BulkDeleteEntitiesAsync(predicate)` inside a transaction scope and returns the number of rows. Unlike the entity overload, it never checks `ISoftDeletedEntity`, so `Customer` rows are physically removed, and it never calls the event publisher, so no deleted events fire. Guest cleanup uses it deliberately.

- The entity overload sets `Deleted = true`; this one does not.
- No per-row events are published.
- No scheduled task is involved; the rows are gone at once.

items.title: Why GetByIdAsync returns a soft-deleted product
items.body:
`GetByIdAsync` declares `bool includeDeleted = true`. Called with only an id, it does not apply the soft-delete filter, so a product with `Deleted = true` is returned like any other. Order history depends on this default; the storefront product page re-checks `product.Deleted` itself and returns 404.

- No filter applies by default, so the result is not null.
- The repository throws nothing for soft-deleted rows.
- The entity is returned as stored; `Deleted` stays true.

items.title: Which Check proves the publisher never throws
items.body:
To prove that the publisher never throws to its caller, point at the `try/catch` around each consumer in `PublishAsync` and at the nested `catch { }` that ignores errors from the logger itself. Together they leave no path for an exception to escape the loop.

- The lock-lifetime arithmetic belongs to the scheduled-task goal.
- The grep for `IConsumer<OrderPlacedEvent>` belongs to listing synchronous checkout work.

items.title: Why an old failure count locks the customer at once
items.body:
While lockout was off, every wrong password still incremented `FailedLoginAttempts`, leaving 7. Changing the setting does not touch stored counters. On the next wrong password the counter becomes 8, and the condition `FailedPasswordAllowedAttempts > 0 && FailedLoginAttempts >= FailedPasswordAllowedAttempts` is 5 > 0 and 8 >= 5, so the customer is locked out immediately for `FailedPasswordLockoutMinutes` and the counter resets to 0.

- Nothing resets counters when an admin edits the setting.
- The comparison is against the stored count, not failures since the change.
- The count is not added to the limit; 8 already meets 5.

items.title: Which Check lists the synchronous checkout work
items.body:
Enumerating the synchronous work in checkout starts from the consumers of `OrderPlacedEvent`: grep for `IConsumer<OrderPlacedEvent>`, find the six files, and classify each handler as a local write, an external HTTP call or a no-op unless configured. They all run inside the checkout request.

- The `try/catch` in `EventPublisher` proves a different goal: that a publish never throws.
- The lock-lifetime arithmetic belongs to scheduled tasks.

items.title: How a null logger skips the remaining consumers
items.body:
The `catch` contains a nested `try` that resolves `ILogger`. If that resolution returns null, the code runs `return;`. A `return` inside a loop body leaves the whole method, not just the current iteration, so consumers three to five never run. In practice the logger always resolves, which is why the guide calls this a latent edge rather than a live bug.

- They do not still run: `return` exits the method.
- Nothing retries a consumer.
- Nothing queues the remaining work.

items.title: Why a rejected add-to-cart still clears checkout choices
items.body:
`AddToCartAsync` calls `ResetCheckoutDataAsync(customer, storeId)` before it looks up the cart item or computes any warnings. That reset clears the selected shipping option, offered options, pickup point, delivery date, payment method and reward-points choice. The out-of-stock warning comes later and returns the warnings, but the reset has already happened. The guide's rule: validate, then mutate.

- The add does have side effects before validation, so the choices are lost.
- The reset does not depend on the cart becoming empty.
- Nothing backs up or restores the cleared data.

items.title: Which login failures share one message
items.body:
The controller's `switch` gives `Deleted`, `NotActive` and `LockedOut` their own localized messages. `CustomerNotExist`, `NotRegistered`, `WrongPassword` and `default` fall through to one case that adds `Account.Login.WrongCredentials`. The generic message hides whether an email exists; the distinct ones do not, which is the enumeration finding F1.

- Deleted, NotActive and LockedOut are exactly the ones with distinct messages.
- Not every failure is generic; three states are revealed.
- WrongPassword is not alone; two other results share its message.

excerpts.quote: case CustomerLoginResults.CustomerNotExist: case CustomerLoginResults.NotRegistered: case CustomerLoginResults.WrongPassword: default:

items.title: Why a failed list update leaves partial changes
items.body:
`UpdateAsync(IList<T>)` calls the provider's `UpdateEntitiesAsync` with no transaction scope, unlike the insert and delete list overloads. The provider loops over the entities and calls `UpdateEntityAsync` for each, and each of those opens its own connection and commits its own statement. When the third update throws, the first two are already committed, and the remaining products are never reached.

- No transaction wraps the list, so nothing is all-or-nothing.
- Nothing catches or retries the failure.
- Committed statements cannot roll back afterwards.

excerpts.quote: foreach (var entity in entities) await UpdateEntityAsync(entity);

items.title: Concept: best-effort side effects and the login gates
items.body:
Chapter 04 asks three questions of every side effect: what if it fails, what if it runs twice, and how would we know? Keep them in mind while reading these files.

- `Nop.Services/Events/EventPublisher.cs`: twenty lines. Trace exactly what happens when a consumer throws, including every statement in the nested `try` inside the `catch`.
- `Nop.Core/Caching/DistributedCacheLocker.cs`: list the cache calls in order. Ask whether anything makes the read and the write one atomic step, and what the `finally` deletes.
- `ScheduleTaskRunner.ExecuteAsync`: work out the lock lifetime formula for a few task periods.

Chapter 03 is about login. In `CustomerRegistrationService.ValidateCustomerAsync`, write down the gates in order and, for the wrong-password branch, which fields change and under which condition. Then read the installer value of `FailedPasswordAllowedAttempts`, and the `switch` in `CustomerController` that turns each result into a message. Finally, in `ShoppingCartService.AddToCartAsync`, note which side effects come before the first warning check.

excerpts.quote: A **side effect** is anything a flow changes beyond its return value — rows, emails, caches, external APIs.
